Treat the two conjuncts independently.

For the first, use the inverse-map characterization of an embedding. The sets \(U_i\cap \operatorname{range}(f)\) form an open cover of \(\operatorname{range}(f)\). If \(f(x)=f(x')\), choose an \(i\) whose \(U_i\) contains this common value; the range hypothesis lifts both \(x,x'\) through \(iV_i\), and injectivity of the embedding \(f\circ iV_i\) gives \(x=x'\). On each \(U_i\cap\operatorname{range}(f)\), the inverse of \(f\) is the restriction of
\[
iV_i\circ (f\circ iV_i)^{-1}.
\]
It is therefore continuous, and these local inverses glue across the open cover. Thus \(f\) is a homeomorphism onto its range.

For the equivalence, prove both universal assertions outright:

- The map \(x\mapsto(U\mapsto x\in U)\) is inducing because the inverse image of the Sierpiński open \(\{\mathrm{true}\}\) under its \(U\)-coordinate is exactly \(U\). Hence its coordinate-induced topology is precisely the original topology on \(X\).
- An embedding \(R\to S\) induces an embedding of matrix spaces by applying it coordinatewise. Restrict this map to the determinant-one subtypes. The relevant square is a pullback: if the image of a matrix has determinant \(1\), then
  \[
  f(\det A)=\det(f(A))=1=f(1),
  \]
  and injectivity of \(f\) implies \(\det A=1\). Embeddings are preserved under this subtype/pullback restriction, yielding the embedding of special linear groups.

The essential algebraic point in the second step is injectivity of the ring homomorphism, supplied by `hf`.
